summary: Describes Adobe's Secure Real-Time Media Flow Protocol (RTMFP), a protocol for securely carrying several parallel flows of real-time video, audio, data and bulk transfers between two endpoints. It is designed to work for peer-to-peer as well as client-server use, including through NAT devices. This is an informational description of a vendor protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a way for two computers to send video, voice and files side by side, safely, even when home routers get in the way.

questions: peer-to-peer media over udp with nat
subtitle: A UDP-based protocol for secure real-time media communication with NAT traversal

tldr.problem: Real-time video and audio applications need low-latency, secure transport that works across NAT boundaries for both peer-to-peer and client-server scenarios, but traditional protocols like TCP and UDP do not handle these requirements well.
tldr.mechanism: RTMFP runs on top of UDP and creates secure bidirectional sessions between endpoints, each session containing independent unidirectional flows with their own reliability, sequencing, and congestion control. Session multiplexing and peer discovery support UDP hole-punching for NAT traversal.
tldr.outcome: Enables real-time media applications to communicate securely over IP networks with multiple parallel flows, addressing both P2P connectivity and traditional client-server deployment.

facts.label: Session multiplexing
facts.value: Multiple sessions per local address using session IDs

facts.label: Flows per session
facts.value: Zero or more unidirectional flows in each direction

facts.label: Reliability options
facts.value: Full, partial, or best-effort per message

facts.label: Congestion control scope
facts.value: Session-level, shared by all sending flows

today: RFC 7016 documents RTMFP as an informational protocol developed outside the IETF standards process. It remains in use in Adobe products for media delivery but is not widely adopted in general internet applications. Modern media protocols like QUIC and WebRTC provide similar capabilities with standards-based development.

sections.title: Design and Motivation
sections.content:
Adobe's Secure Real-Time Media Flow Protocol (RTMFP) is a general-purpose endpoint-to-endpoint transport service built on UDP that was originally developed by Adobe Systems to support real-time media delivery in Flash Player, Adobe AIR, and Adobe Media Server. It was designed to address limitations of existing protocols when delivering video and audio with low latency while supporting both client-server and peer-to-peer communication. RTMFP treats security as a fundamental building block: the security framework is built into the protocol itself, allowing each application to define its own cryptographic algorithms and parameters through a Cryptography Profile.

Key design goals include minimizing wasted bytes and round trips, supporting multiple independent message flows with different reliability and priority settings within a single session, enabling NAT traversal through UDP hole-punching, and providing built-in congestion control. The protocol is fundamentally message-oriented rather than stream-oriented, allowing applications to control message boundaries and choose delivery guarantees on a per-message basis.
sections.plainLanguage: Adobe built a tunnel on top of UDP that can send multiple message types at different priorities, encrypt everything, and find its way through home routers.

sections.title: Sessions and Message Flows
sections.content:
RTMFP communication is organized into two levels. A session is a bidirectional, secured, congestion-controlled connection between two endpoints. Within each session are flows, which are unidirectional message streams from one endpoint to the other. An endpoint can have multiple sessions with different far endpoints, and within each session there can be zero or more flows in each direction. Each flow is named with arbitrary user-defined metadata rather than fixed port or stream numbers, providing flexibility for application-specific naming.

Each flow has its own sequence number space independent of other flows, and messages within a flow can be sent with full reliability (like TCP), partial reliability, or best effort (like UDP). Messages can be delivered to the receiving application in the original order sent or in network arrival order, a choice the receiver makes. This combination allows different types of traffic (video, audio, text) with different requirements to coexist in a single session, with each flow's delivery guarantees and ordering determined by the application's needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a session as a tunnel and flows as different-colored streams inside it. Each stream carries different types of messages with different delivery promises.

sections.title: Session Establishment and NAT Traversal
sections.content:
A session begins with a handshake where the initiator sends an Initiator Hello (IHello) chunk containing its endpoint discriminator and preferred address, which the responder receives and uses to form a Responder Hello (RHello). During this exchange, the endpoints exchange Diffie-Hellman public keys and other parameters needed for the security framework. The protocol supports several mechanisms to traverse NAT devices: if both endpoints are behind NAT, each sends packets to the other's suspected address; the responder may redirect the initiator to a different address if needed; and a forwarder mechanism allows an endpoint outside NAT to help introduction.

Session identifiers (session IDs) allow an endpoint to multiplex many sessions over a single local transport address while allowing sessions to survive changes in transport address, important for mobile and wireless deployments. The cryptographic endpoint discriminator resists port scanning by requiring knowledge of the session's secret material to form valid packets. All control messages and data are encrypted according to the cryptography profile defined by the application, with only the IP network addresses and session identifier visible in the clear.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake is like saying hello through a wall, exchanging secret codes, and figuring out how to reach each other if routers are in the way.

sections.title: Reliability, Sequencing, and Congestion Control
sections.content:
Each message sent on a flow is independently assigned a sequence number and can have a different reliability requirement. The sender fragments large messages into chunks that fit in UDP packets, assigning each chunk a sequence number. The receiver acknowledges received data using either Bitmap Ack chunks (compact bit patterns) or Range Ack chunks (lists of ranges) depending on the loss pattern. If a sender does not receive acknowledgements within a timeout window, it retransmits the lost data.

Congestion control operates at the session level, shared by all sending flows from one endpoint. The protocol uses round-trip time measurements, acknowledgement feedback, and a configurable congestion control algorithm (an example algorithm is provided in the RFC). Each flow has its own receive window for flow control, allowing independent management of buffer resources. Retransmission timeouts start conservatively and are calculated based on measured round-trip time, with burst avoidance mechanisms to prevent network congestion. Time-critical reverse notifications allow a receiver to signal congestion back to the sender as soon as data loss or buffer fill is detected.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a number and a reliability promise. Lost messages are resent. Multiple messages share the network fairly, and receivers tell senders to slow down if data piles up.

sections.title: Packet Structure and Optimization
sections.content:
RTMFP packets are built from a network layer header followed by one or more chunks. The network layer header contains the session ID and optionally cryptographic material for the first message in a session (containing public keys and nonces for key derivation). Subsequent packets in an established session contain only the session ID and encrypted content, minimizing header overhead. All payload data, headers, and control information (except network addresses and session ID) are encrypted according to the Cryptography Profile.

Variable-length unsigned integer (VLU) encoding is used throughout the protocol to minimize wasted bytes: integers that fit in fewer bits are encoded using fewer bytes. Chunks include various types: fragment chunks carry message fragments, hello and keying chunks establish sessions, ping/pong chunks measure round-trip time and detect address changes, user data chunks carry application messages, acknowledgement chunks confirm received data, and close chunks terminate sessions. The protocol avoids 32-bit alignment constraints, packing structures tightly to reduce bandwidth consumption.
sections.plainLanguage: Packets are stacked with a small header and several chunks, each handling different jobs. Everything is squeezed tight to waste no bytes, and encrypted so only the right recipient can read it.
